result: The hemibrain dataset represents the largest dense reconstruction to date, containing approximately 25,000 neurons and 20 million chemical synapses, covering 36% of all synaptic neuropils and 54% of central brain neuropils by volume, with a total size of 26 teravoxels.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C20 provide consistent quantitative descriptions of the dataset's scale and coverage. These are straightforward descriptive statistics about the dataset that are explicitly stated and internally consistent. The claims are supported by the accompanying figure and table data showing the reconstruction volume and neuron counts.

result: The sample preparation involved a 5-day-old female fly dissected 1.5 hr after lights-on, with the brain sectioned into 37 sagittal slabs of 20 μm thickness using hot-knife sectioning with ~30 nm material loss between slabs, and 13 consecutive slabs imaged at 8×8×8 nm voxel resolution using FIB-SEM.
evaluation: Claims C6-C13 describe the methodological pipeline from specimen preparation through imaging. These claims are explicit, internally consistent, and provide specific technical parameters. The cited reference (C11) for neural process dimensions (15-50 nm) appropriately justifies the chosen imaging resolution of 8 nm voxels.

result: Automated segmentation using flood-filling networks trained on ~5 billion voxels achieved an expected run length (ERL) of 163 μm with 0.25% false merge rate before agglomeration, which increased to 585 μm ERL but with 27.6% false merge rate after agglomeration.
evaluation: Claims C14-C16 provide quantitative metrics for segmentation quality at different stages. The trade-off between run length and false merge rate after agglomeration is explicitly stated and represents a known challenge in connectomics. The metrics are standard for evaluating segmentation quality and the values are plausible given the methodology described.

result: The hemibrain contains over 9 million T-bars and 60 million PSDs, with an average of 6.7 PSDs per T-bar, reflecting the polyadic nature of Drosophila synapses.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19 describe synapse counts and their ratio. The arithmetic is correct (64M PSDs / 9.5M T-bars ≈ 6.7), and the polyadic nature of Drosophila synapses is well-established in the literature (C52). The values are consistent with the known biology and the imaging methodology.

result: The reconstruction identified 22,594 neurons comprising 5,229 morphological types and 5,609 connectivity types, with 15,912 neurons traced to cell bodies and 192 distinct cell body fiber (CBF) bundles identified, of which 155 matched 92 known and 6 newly identified clonal units.
evaluation: Claims C21-C25 provide a comprehensive census of neurons and cell types. The numbers are internally consistent and the identification of new clonal units (C25) validates the completeness of the reconstruction. The large number of single-instance types (C22) is acknowledged and explained as likely having contralateral partners.

result: Synapse prediction accuracy showed median precision of 88% for both upstream and downstream connections, with 90% of cell types achieving at least 70% accuracy, and mean synapse precision of 76.1% for single-connection pathways across 57 brain regions.
evaluation: Claims C26-C29 provide comprehensive validation metrics for synapse detection. The consistency between upstream and downstream precision (both 88%) and the separate validation of single-connection pathways (76.1%) provide multiple lines of evidence for accuracy. The slightly lower precision for single connections is expected and acknowledged.

result: The fly brain exhibits short path lengths with three-quarters of neuron pairs connected by fewer than three interneurons, and connection strength distribution follows a power law with exponent -1.67 and exponential cutoff at N=42, differing from log-normal distributions found in mammalian cortex.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33 describe network topology and connection strength distributions. The short path lengths are well-documented in the data (Figure 20), and the power law distribution is explicitly fitted and contrasted with mammalian findings (C32). The comparison acknowledges methodological differences between studies, appropriately qualifying the interpretation.

result: Network motif analysis revealed over-representation of reciprocal connections across all brain regions, with only a few cell types forming large cliques (primarily ring neurons in the central complex), and bidirectional one-to-many connectivity motifs found in 73 cells across 22 types in the CX, 19 cells across 14 types in optic lobe, and 12 types across 9 types in MB.
evaluation: Claims C34-C39 describe network motifs with specific quantitative data. The over-representation of reciprocal connections (C34) is confirmed across regions and cites supporting literature. The clique analysis (C35-C36) is specific and includes Table 5 with detailed statistics. The one-to-many motif counts (C37-C39) are explicit and region-specific.

result: Electrical modeling demonstrates that the anatomically-defined compartment structure of the fly brain directly corresponds to the electrical response properties of neurons, with compartment boundaries showing clear separation in signal delays and amplitudes.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 present conclusions from electrical modeling (Figure 25). The modeling approach is described in detail with appropriate biophysical parameters (Table 6), and the results show clear separation between intra- and inter-compartment responses. The conclusion that anatomical compartments match electrical compartments is supported by the quantitative analysis showing 10-fold improvement in delay prediction accuracy using compartment-based models.

result: Rent's rule analysis shows that almost all fly brain compartments fall within the range of Rent exponents (0.5-0.7) expected for packing-dominated systems, with only the ellipsoid body falling just outside this range, suggesting both biological and human-designed systems are dominated by similar packing considerations.
evaluation: Claims C42-C43 present quantitative Rent's rule analysis with explicit comparison to human-designed systems (Figure 26). The analysis is methodologically sound, comparing T-bars (computation) to neuron crossings (connections). Claim C44 is appropriately presented as speculation ('A natural speculation'), acknowledging the inferential nature of the evolutionary interpretation while being supported by the quantitative similarity in Rent exponents.

result: Registration analysis reveals that the hemibrain EM data is 17% larger than the 2014 confocal atlas and 30% larger than the JRC2018 template, with angular tilts of 18.5° and 14° respectively between these reference frames.
evaluation: Claims C45-C48 describe quantitative differences between imaging modalities and reference frames. The size differences are explicitly stated with citations (C45-C46) and shown in Figure 19. The angular measurements (C47-C48) are specific and necessary for accurate registration. These differences are expected due to different preparation methods and are appropriately documented.

result: The raw image data exceeds 20 TB requiring 2 days to download at 1 Gb/s, and scaling calculations indicate a mouse brain at similar resolution would require almost 1000 petabytes.
evaluation: Claims C49-C50 provide explicit data size and transfer time metrics that are straightforward to verify (20 TB / 1 Gb/s ≈ 2 days). Claim C51 extrapolates to mouse brain based on volume scaling (500 mm³ vs ~0.03 mm³ for hemibrain) and cites supporting literature. The calculation is reasonable given the ~16,000-fold volume difference, though it assumes similar resolution and tissue properties.

result: About 5% of connections with strength ≥6 synapses are distributed across two or more non-adjacent compartments, representing parallel connections in separate brain regions.
evaluation: Claim C30 quantifies a specific connectivity motif with explicit threshold criteria. This is supported by the dense reconstruction enabling identification of all synapses and their compartment locations. The biological significance is discussed in relation to electrical modeling (Figure 24b), showing these connections have different response properties than single-compartment connections.

result: All hemibrain data are publicly available through web interfaces including NeuPrint, designed for query access without specialized training.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 describe data accessibility and cite the NeuPrint publication (Clements et al., 2020). The claims are verifiable and represent an important aspect of the resource. The emphasis on accessibility without specialized training is a key feature distinguishing this from previous connectomics efforts.

result: The hemibrain region was selected because it contains all central brain circuits (assuming bilateral symmetry), including those critical for associative learning (mushroom body), navigation and sleep (central complex), and circadian rhythms, while previous dense reconstructions have shown that cell type catalogs are incomplete and circuitry depends on age, nutrition, and circadian state.
evaluation: Claims C55-C60 provide scientific justification for the region selection and acknowledge limitations. C55 cites prior work (Takemura et al., 2017) showing incomplete catalogs. C56 acknowledges known sources of variability. C57-C60 explicitly state the rationale for region selection based on functional circuits of interest. These claims appropriately contextualize the study design.

result: Version v1.1 includes improvements in accuracy and naming consistency, while acknowledging limitations including inability to detect gap junctions at the resolution used, difficulty segmenting glial cells, and exclusion of autapses due to high false positive rates.
evaluation: Claims C61-C65 transparently describe both improvements and limitations. C61 documents version updates. C62-C65 explicitly acknowledge what is not included in the dataset and why, which is critical for appropriate interpretation. The reasoning for excluding autapses (C64-C65) is sound given they fall below false positive rates.

result: Fly nervous systems differ from vertebrates in several aspects, including examples like the APL neuron regulating Kenyon cell sparseness through bidirectional connections, and PEN1/PEN2 neurons having similar morphology but distinct inputs and functional activity.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 describe biological differences with appropriate citations. C66 cites a review (Meinertzhagen, 2016b). C67 describes the well-known APL neuron with citation (Lin et al., 2014). C68-C69 provide a specific example of connectivity-based cell type distinction with supporting functional data (Green et al., 2017), demonstrating the value of connectivity information beyond morphology.

result: The asymmetrical body (AB) is a small structure adjacent to the fan-shaped body showing left-right asymmetry, with the hemibrain specimen having ABs on both sides (right: 1679 μm³, left: 526 μm³), consistent with the 7.6% of wild-type flies reported to have bilateral ABs, though absolute sizes differ from light microscopy measurements (522 μm³ right, 126 μm³ left, n=21).
evaluation: Claims C70-C75 describe the AB with specific measurements and appropriate citations. The size measurements (C72-C74) are explicit and show clear asymmetry. The comparison with light microscopy data (C75) appropriately notes both consistency in asymmetry pattern and differences in absolute size, which could reflect methodological differences or individual variation. The citation of prior work (C71) provides context.

result: Detailed compartmentalization is provided for major brain structures: the mushroom body has 15 compartments (α1-3, α'1-3, β1-2, β'1-2, γ1-5), the fan-shaped body has 9 horizontal layers (FBl1-9), the ellipsoid body has 7 non-overlapping zones, and 41 types of LC, 2 types of LPC, 6 types of LLPC, and 3 types of LPLC visual projection neurons were identified.
evaluation: Claims C76-C79 provide detailed anatomical compartmentalization with appropriate citations. The mushroom body (C76) and fan-shaped body (C77) compartments cite established literature (Tanaka et al., 2008; Aso et al., 2014; Wolff et al., 2015). The ellipsoid body zones (C78) are defined based on ring neuron innervation patterns shown in Figure 7G. The visual projection neuron counts (C79) represent an exhaustive identification within the volume.

result: More than 500 examples of cells connecting unidirectionally (either to or from, but not both) to all cells of a given type were found across many brain regions.
evaluation: Claim C81 quantifies a common connectivity motif. This is a straightforward count from the dense reconstruction and represents the least constrained of the large motifs analyzed (compared to cliques or bidirectional connections). The number is plausible given the scale of the reconstruction and the explicit statement that this motif is 'very common.'

result: Different neurons show varying degrees of compartmentalization in their computations: CT1 neurons perform independent computations in each branch, medulla neurons likely perform single computations due to insignificant delays, and PEN2 neuron compartments in the protocerebral bridge respond differently from those in the ellipsoid body.
evaluation: Claims C82-C84 cite specific prior studies demonstrating functional compartmentalization (Meier and Borst, 2019; Takemura et al., 2013; Green et al., 2017; Turner-Evans et al., 2019). These examples provide biological context for the electrical modeling results (C40-C41) and demonstrate that anatomical compartments can correspond to functional compartments, though the degree varies by neuron type.
